newsitem.title: TAIWAN: BASEBALL-GAME-FIXING SCANDALS SOIL TAIWAN'S PASTIME.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-GAME-FIXING SCANDALS SOIL TAIWAN'S PASTIME.

text.p: Kuo Shang-hao, a star pitcher for Taiwan's President Lions who rarely loses, took the mound last August 28 intending to do just that. Working with a group of gangsters to fix the game, Kuo -- normally an excellent pitcher and the most valuable player in the seven-team Chinese Professional Baseball League for 1996 -- duly put his team in a hole before being sent to the bench. However, the Lions eventually recovered to beat the Sinon Bulls 12-7, causing Kuo and his mobster cohorts to lose more than T$100 million (US$4 million).

But Kuo's troubles were only beginning. In May, 13 CPBL players -- including Kuo, former U.S. Major League pitcher Ravelo Manzanillo, and Chiang Tai-chuan, the respected captain of Taiwan's 1992 Olympic silver-medal winning team -- were indicted on a range of corruption charges related to game-fixing. The charges, which allege that more than a dozen games in 1996 were fixed by players in conspir acy with Taiwan's notorious underworld, crowned a year of shocking revelations and rumours that have stunned followers of the island's most popular sport. Prosecutors say they suspect more players are involved and vow to press ahead with investigations, part of a wide crackdown on what many c

Baseball has always been the king of sports on an island whose youth teams regularly win the Little League World Series in the U.S. in convincing fashion and which exulted in the Olympic team's success in Barcelona.

Taiwan's baseball stars are idolised and well compensated for their efforts, with top players making around T$400,000 (US$14,300) per month over 12 months. But the sensational game-fixing disclosures have shredded the wholesome reputation of the island's beloved game.

"Rumours started surfacing in the second half of last season that organised crime was involved in baseball gambling," Daniel Tu, secretary general of the seven-year-old league, told Reuters in a recent interview.
"To be frank, I think it's a big problem," Tu said.
Tu said the scandals have jeopardised the game's integrity and caused a decline in fan attendance, though no figures are yet available.
"The greatest impact on our league and the game has been the lack of trust and confidence of the fans," said Tu.
The government's charges paint a picture of top players being strong-armed by Taiwan's powerful mafia.
One allegation speaks of four gangsters -- one a policeman -- coercing a player at gunpoint into throwing games to pay off gambling debts.
Another describes gangsters cornering and roughing up three players after a game that did not turn out as the gangsters had intended.
"We are making these allegations after a year of careful fact-finding," said Huang Po-lin, the prosecutor who spearheaded the investigations.
"We also are investigating additional cases of possible game-fixing," he told Reuters in an interview.
Huang said he could not comment further on the continuing probe before formal charges are filed against those suspected of wrongdoing.
The league has suspended all indicted players pending court verdicts.

Manzanillo, who played briefly for Taiwan's China Times in 1996 after a stint with the Pittsburg Pirates in the United States, left the island before being indicted. Huang said his office did not know of Manzanillo's whereabouts.

Kuo, who helped the President Lions to an allegedly tainted championship in 1996, signed with the CPBL's fledgling rival league, the four-team Taiwan Major League, shortly after allegations of his involvement in game-fixing began to surface.
But the new league, hoping to stay unsullied in the scandal, has not allowed Kuo to take the field with other high-salaried stars poached from the older league.
"We absolutely emphasise that this is a new beginning, with real games," said Taiwan Major League president Joey Chen. "This (game-fixing) is something that the fans cannot forgive."
Tu has urged the government to lift a long-time ban on legal gambling as a way to prevent organised crime from manipulating games from behind the scenes.
"We know the money being wagered on professional baseball here in Taiwan is enormous. Some have even said a couple of billion U.S. dollars are being wagered per season," Tu said.
"As long as the wagering does not involve players, coaches or umpires and does not alter the outcome of the game, I would be willing to consider it," Tu said.
The government has vowed to consider the proposal.
For now, both leagues say they will seek to stamp out game-fixing by setting up task forces to monitor games for irregularities.
